Definition: Reflective roof products, installation, quality checks and recoating services intended to reduce solar heat gain.
Who pays: Owners, landlords, employers, housing authorities; grants/public purchasers for low-income stock.
Who benefits: Residents, tenants, home-based workers, pupils and clinic users.
Business models: Materials retail; Installed roof contract; Maintenance/recoating agreement; Public or NGO bulk procurement
How: Subsidised/community retrofits can reach low-income occupants; roof control, rent and upkeep matter. No poorest-quintile reach verified.
Cycles: The cooling trap; The energy-poverty trap; The sleepless-nights loop; The poverty–heat trap

Definition: Shading, insulation, ventilation design, glazing, ceilings and heat-resilient retrofit/construction services; excludes roof coatings already assigned above.
Who pays: Developers, building owners, employers, schools, health/public housing departments.
Who benefits: Occupants, including renters and home-based workers.
Business models: Design/engineering fees; Materials and construction contracts; Retrofit bundles; Public housing procurement
How: Public/social-housing procurement can provide access; informal tenure and permissions may prevent otherwise cheap works.
Cycles: The sleepless-nights loop; The lost-schooling loop; The cooling trap; The energy-poverty trap; The displacement loop

Part of the economy: Outdoor shade, urban greening and plant care
Definition: Shade structures, trees, green roofs/walls and planting/irrigation/maintenance services with a documented cooling purpose.
Who pays: Cities, landowners, schools, developers and employers; public/grant support for shared spaces.
Who benefits: Pedestrians, vendors, outdoor workers and neighbours.
Business models: Design-build contracts; Landscape maintenance services; Public-space concessions with safeguards; Community stewardship paid contracts
How: Free public shade can benefit poor users; siting, accessible routes and anti-displacement measures determine reach.
Cycles: The dying-green loop; The green-displacement loop; The cooling trap; The poverty–heat trap

Part of the economy: Efficient fans and low-energy air movement
Definition: Ceiling, table, pedestal and ventilation fans, including efficient motors, installation and repair.
Who pays: Households, employers, schools, clinics and public procurement agencies.
Who benefits: Room occupants and workers with access to power and controls.
Business models: Appliance sale; Institutional bulk supply; Repair and maintenance; Targeted subsidy or lease
How: Lower upfront/running costs than some refrigerated systems can help, but no poorest-quintile affordability proof was established. Shared/public procurement can bridge access.
Cycles: The energy-poverty trap; The sleepless-nights loop; The cooling trap; The global cooling loop

Definition: Direct and indirect evaporative coolers, wet-media systems and their installation/cleaning services.
Who pays: Households, workshops, warehouses, employers and institutional buyers.
Business models: Equipment sale; Installed industrial ventilation contract; Pad/water-system servicing
How: Lower-cost models may improve access in suitable dry conditions; water and upkeep can still make them unaffordable.
Cycles: The energy-poverty trap; The cooling trap; The energy–water loop

Part of the economy: Efficient room and small-building air conditioning
Definition: Efficient inverter/split/window and packaged refrigeration-based cooling, installation, controls and repair; district systems are separate.
Who pays: Households, landlords, employers, education/health agencies and facility owners.
Who benefits: Users of cooled rooms; access is not implied by city-wide appliance sales.
Business models: Equipment sale and installation; Maintenance contract; Institutional procurement; Targeted voucher or service contract
How: Targeted subsidies or public cool rooms can help; tariffs, outages, tenure and installation barriers remain.
Cycles: The cooling trap; The global cooling loop; The energy-poverty trap; The sleepless-nights loop; The overwhelmed-clinic loop

Definition: Refrigerant supply, technician training, leak detection, safe maintenance, reclamation and end-of-life recovery for cooling equipment.
Who pays: Equipment owners, servicing firms, manufacturers and compliance programmes.
Who benefits: Cooling users, technicians and communities benefiting from safer lower-emission systems.
Business models: Service call and maintenance fees; Refrigerant recovery/reclamation fees; Technician training contracts; Producer responsibility procurement
How: Indirect reach through maintained affordable appliances; technician coverage and owner ability to pay determine access.
Cycles: The global cooling loop; The cooling trap

Definition: Central chilled-water networks and long-term building cooling services, including storage when contracted within the cooling asset.
Who pays: Developers, building owners, commercial tenants and public anchor customers.
Business models: Cooling capacity and usage charges; Design-build-own-operate concession; Energy/service performance contract
How: Commercial-campus transactions do not demonstrate access for informal settlements; public anchor demand and tariff safeguards would need separate design.
Cycles: The cooling trap; The global cooling loop; The energy–water loop

Part of the economy: Distributed food and medical cold chains
Definition: Off-grid/weak-grid cold rooms, precooling, refrigerated transport and medical refrigeration with appropriate separate standards.
Who pays: Farmers/traders/FPOs, food businesses, public health purchasers and logistics clients.
Who benefits: Growers, vendors, consumers and patients; benefit allocation depends on fees and bargaining power.
Business models: Equipment sale; Pay-per-crate/day storage; Lease or rental; Transport and cold-chain service contracts; Medical public procurement
How: Pay-per-use reduces equipment ownership barriers, but the poorest may lack produce volumes, transport or cash. Medical access normally requires institutional funding.
Cycles: The farm-debt loop; The heat credit squeeze; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The energy–water loop

Part of the economy: Personal cooling and cooled worker recovery
Definition: Cooling garments, conductive/phase-change systems and portable cooled recovery services used as additions to environmental and work protection.
Who pays: Employers and institutional buyers; sometimes individual workers.
Who benefits: Workers and caregivers; applicability varies by health, clothing and task.
Business models: Equipment/PPE sale; Rental and recharge service; Employer recovery-area service contract
How: Employer-paid provision can reach low-paid workers; self-purchase and unpaid recharge time exclude others.
Cycles: The poverty–heat trap; The overwhelmed-clinic loop

Part of the economy: Heat exposure sensors and WBGT monitoring
Definition: Instrument sales, rental, calibration, indoor monitoring and exposure dashboards tied to an actionable response.
Who pays: Employers, institutions, cities and research/public programmes.
Who benefits: Workers/occupants and decision-makers; protection depends on response.
Business models: Instrument sale; Rental/calibration contract; Managed sensing subscription; Institutional monitoring service
How: Institutional/collective purchase can cover informal or poor communities; retail wearable access is unverified.
Cycles: The invisible-deaths loop; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The poverty–heat trap

Part of the economy: Heat-risk intelligence, early warnings and decision support
Definition: Heat forecasts, risk analytics, APIs, local thresholds, translation and last-mile warning-to-action services, including heat analytics for lenders/cities.
Who pays: Cities, employers, lenders/insurers, public weather/health programmes and research buyers.
Who benefits: Decision-makers and people reached by protective actions; alerts alone are not benefit.
Business models: Enterprise API/SaaS subscription; Public service contract; Open public infrastructure with funded local delivery
How: Public/local-language/offline distribution can reach poor users; subscription-only products and smartphone delivery are insufficient.
Cycles: The reactive-spending loop; The invisible-deaths loop; The poverty–heat trap; The heat credit squeeze

Part of the economy: Parametric heat insurance and income-risk services
Definition: Insurance underwriting, distribution, triggers, claims/payment administration and independent assessment for heat-driven income losses.
Who pays: Workers/collectives, employers, public sponsors, premium-support grants and risk carriers.
Who benefits: Insured people/enterprises; non-enrolled users are excluded.
Business models: Premium-funded insurance; Group policy distribution; Sponsor-supported cover; Risk modelling/payment service contracts
How: Group enrolment and premium support may help; current premium support and poorest-quintile reach were not verified for the cited example.
Cycles: The protection-gap loop; The poverty–heat trap; The heat credit squeeze

Part of the economy: Cooling access finance, leasing and aggregation
Definition: Cooling-specific credit, leases, on-bill/PAYG contracts, bulk buying and guarantees enabling eligible cooling purchases; underlying equipment remains in its product segment.
Who pays: Borrowers/lessees, employers, institutional buyers, public sponsors and lenders.
Who benefits: Eligible users of financed cooling; excluded applicants require another route.
Business models: Installment credit; Operating lease; On-bill or PAYG contracts; Guarantee-backed lending; Demand aggregation fees
How: Unstable income, informal tenure and lack of meters can exclude the poorest even with smaller installments; assess disposable income and service continuity.
Cycles: The energy-poverty trap; The heat credit squeeze; The protection-gap loop

Part of the economy: Heat-protection drinking water and water services
Definition: Safe drinking-water refill, storage, filtration, maintenance and backup supply explicitly serving hot workplaces, clinics and public heat protection.
Who pays: Employers, municipalities, schools/clinics, utilities or supported community operators.
Who benefits: Workers, patients, pupils, vendors and people travelling in heat.
Business models: Water service/maintenance contract; Employer refill supply; Publicly purchased free distribution; Regulated refill fee with safeguards
How: Free safe points and accessible sanitation can help poor users; paid water can exclude them during the hottest hours.
Cycles: The energy–water loop; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The poverty–heat trap

Part of the economy: Workplace heat compliance and protection services
Definition: Risk assessment, work-rest protocols, training, inspection support, worker representation, schedule design and implementation assurance; devices are separate products.
Who pays: Employers, brands/buyers, public labour agencies and supported worker organisations.
Who benefits: Workers, including low-paid and subcontracted staff if actually covered.
Business models: OSH consulting/training contract; Employer managed service; Buyer-financed supplier programme; Public inspection/worker-support budget
How: Reaches informal workers only if employers, buyers or public programmes cover them; ordinary compliance markets may miss them.
Cycles: The poverty–heat trap; The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The protection-gap loop

Part of the economy: Heat-resilient crop inputs and farm advice
Definition: Heat-tolerant seed, licensing/multiplication and heat-specific agronomic advice; farm fans, shade and storage retain their equipment segment.
Who pays: Farmers/FPOs, seed distributors, public extension and procurement programmes.
Who benefits: Growers, farm households and food consumers; worker protection needs separate measures.
Business models: Seed sale/licensing; Community multiplication; Extension/advisory contracts; Public seed/extension support
How: Public/community seed channels may reach low-income growers; landless workers may gain little without labour protection.
Cycles: The farm-debt loop; The dry-soil loop; The poverty–heat trap

Part of the economy: Heat-ready health and care delivery services
Definition: Facility preparedness, emergency cooling procurement, staff training, surveillance support and continuity of care explicitly addressing heat.
Who pays: Public health budgets, facility owners, health systems and donors; avoid relying on emergency patient fees.
Who benefits: Patients, caregivers and health workers, especially those unable to pay.
Business models: Facility retrofit/service contract; Clinical training procurement; Maintenance/standby service; Publicly funded care provision
How: Public/free care and accessible outreach can reach poor people; private fee-for-service cooling/care may exclude them. No universal free-treatment entitlement inferred.
Cycles: The overwhelmed-clinic loop; The invisible-deaths loop; The medical-debt trap; The reactive-spending loop

Part of the economy: Cooling power resilience, controls and thermal storage
Definition: Cooling-specific demand response, controls, backup design and thermal/electrical storage integration; generic solar is excluded without a cooling use case.
Who pays: Utilities, aggregators, facility owners, employers and public infrastructure purchasers.
Who benefits: Cooling users and system customers; vulnerable users need exclusion/override protections.
Business models: Demand-response aggregation/service fee; Control/maintenance subscription; Storage project contract; Critical-facility resilience procurement
How: Most offers require controllable assets, meters and connectivity; poor households may be excluded or harmed by unsafe curtailment.
Cycles: The energy–water loop; The cooling trap; The overwhelmed-clinic loop
